newsitem.title: USA: Centennial sees turnaround from financial scandal.
newsitem.headline: Centennial sees turnaround from financial scandal.

text.p: Centennial Technologies Inc.'s interim chief executive said Tuesday the company, whose founder sits in jail on insider trading charges, should be an "easy turnaround" and customers are staying loyal.

Lawrence Ramaekers, who last week replaced founder Emanuel Pinez after he was charged with insider trading and who allegedly recorded phony sales, said in an interview that most of Centennial's sales were legitimate.
"Last week I think we had an exceptional record in sales," he said in a telephone interview. "The customers, and I've talked to a bunch of them, and they're all staying with us," he said.
The Securities and Exchange Commission has alleged that Pinez changed inventory tags to record fictitious sales, thereby inflating Centennial's reported results to meet analysts expectations.

Centennial, the best performing stock on the New York Stock Exchange last year, said earlier this month it will have to restate earnings for the first half of 1997 and for 1996 and will report a loss for those periods instead of a profit.
Stock in the Billerica, Mass.-based manufacturer of personal computer memory cards ended 1996 at $55, tumbled following news of the accounting improprieties to a low of $1.75.
Over the last two days, Centennial's stock has climbed higher, but Ramaekers said he did not know why specifically, but shareholders may be recognising the value of the company.

On Tuesday, Centennial's stock shot tripled, rising $9 to $13.50 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the most active issue. The NYSE has said it will de-list the company on March 3 because of the false earnings statements.
After a week of talking to nervous customers, employees and banks, Ramaekers said he thought "almost all of Centennial sales are real sales."

He also has travelled to check into the legitimacy of a many small companies Centennial had invested in or bought, but he still did not know the number of companies or their exact relationship with Centennial.
Ramaekers is a principal of turnaround specialists Jay Alix & Associates of Southfield, Mich.
He served as an excutive most recently with Ryder Truck Rental Systems Inc., Colour Tile Inc., and Family Restaurants and consulted in turning around Wang Laboratories Inc. and Unisys Corp..

"The difference with Centennial is that this does not appear to be a business problem," he said. "It appears to be a group of successful businesses and it should be an easy turnaround once we get everything stabilised."
The Securities and Exchange Commission said it was continuing its investigation into Centennial, but Ramaekers said he was confident most of the company's problems have been exposed.

"I think that everything that is going to be uncovered other than finalising what the numbers are has already been stated somewhere in the press," he said. "The employees, everybody that's still here, I have a lot of confidence in them."
BankBoston Corp., whose chief financial officer sits on the Centennial board of directors and is the primary banker, has been lending the company cash on an ongoing basis, he said.
Two accounting firms are investigating the company, and Ramaekers said he did not know a date when Centennial would be able to release its restated earnings.
